source.title: Hierarchical Dual-Strategy Unlearning for Biomedical and Healthcare Intelligence Using Imperfect and Privacy-Sensitive Medical Data
source.authors: Yi Zhang; Chao Zhang; Zijian Li; Tian-Xiang Xu; Kunyu Zhang; Zhang-Yang Gao; Meinuo Li; Xiaohan Zhang; Qi-Chao Qi; Bingjie Chen

record.file_problem: The full text is present. The paper includes some apparent formatting or terminology inconsistencies, but the relevant results are readable.
record.tranche_reason: It reports the effects of its own and baseline unlearning methods on targeted medical knowledge and retained ability. It does not test whether attacks recover the unlearned knowledge.
record.gate_note: No fine-tuning recovery attack, activation-direction ablation, quantization attack, or prompt-rephrasing/jailbreak attack is reported. The paper's MIA results measure membership-inference resistance, not recovery of targeted knowledge by the attacks in claim versions B–E. No rows are recorded for those measures. Cited results from other work are not recorded.
record.test_reason: In a new medical setting (Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, MedMCQA surgery and MHQA anxiety), it reports targeted accuracy after unlearning and retained accuracy on other domains. That bears only on the first part of version A. No recovery attack (fine-tuning, internal edits, quantization, prompting) is run, so B–F and A's 'attacks don't recover it' clause are untested.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly right: the authors conclude their hierarchical dual-strategy method removes surgical (and anxiety) knowledge (82.7% FR) while preserving other medical knowledge (88.5%), with DP privacy and 0.1% parameter updates. They do not address recovery attacks or whether knowledge is deleted rather than suppressed.
record.recipe_differences: Introduces geometric-constrained gradient updates, concept-aware token interventions, LoRA, and differential privacy for medical-domain unlearning; it does not implement or evaluate the recovery attacks in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports differences across unlearning methods and between the MedMCQA surgical target and MHQA anxiety target. It also describes sensitivity to hierarchy weights, but those values are discussed as a method analysis rather than recovery-attack tests.

fits_no_version.finding: Membership-inference AUC after unlearning (proposed method 0.555, original 0.98; Table V), and MIA resistance on MHQA (Table VII).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Unlearning lowers membership-inference detectability of forget-set examples. This is privacy leakage, not recovery of targeted knowledge.

record.peer_reviewed: IEEE transactions on consumer electronics (venue as supplied)
record.problems: No chance-level baseline is stated for targeted accuracy. The study evaluates only one named foundation model and does not test post-unlearning knowledge recovery. The reported MIA measures are not recovery tests of versions B–E.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for MIA resistance, privacy risk, DP strength, HMTA, unlearning score, hierarchy separation, or efficiency metrics: these do not measure the targeted-knowledge recovery or the general-ability measures named in version A. No results from ablations or sensitivity analyses are included where they only compare components or parameter settings of the paper's new method.

untested.parts: Whether simple attacks (fine-tuning, prompting, quantization, probing) fail to recover the removed surgical or anxiety knowledge; no attack is run.
All: no activation ablation or probing of whether knowledge is blocked or deleted.
All: no rephrasing, jailbreak, cross-lingual or in-context recovery.
All: the new method is not evaluated against recovery attacks; MIA resistance is not knowledge recovery.

missing.what: Per-subdomain retention accuracies after unlearning (internal medicine 91.8, pediatrics 94.1, obs/gyn 88.7) against surgery 17.3; bears on A's general-ability clause.

record.verdict_notes: All reader row links used the invalid version 'V1'; they are relinked to A, or to 'none' for Original-Model and Complete-Retraining reference rows. The reader's 'partial' on target rows is wrong: MedMCQA is 4-option, so 17–27% is at or below chance. The paper states no chance level. The study is evidence only for A's surface clause, so it says nothing about shallowness. Below-chance accuracy (17.3%) could reflect active answer suppression, but this is untested. Internal inconsistencies lower confidence in the numbers: FR 0 for the original model despite 89.2% accuracy, then FR 82.7 = 100−17.3; Original Model 'US' 44.6; Qwen described as 'pre-trained on medical literature'; p<0.001 claimed from 3 seeds. Reported p-values and statistics are unverifiable. Only one model is tested.

versions.untested_parts: Tests targeted performance reduction and retention, but not whether simple attacks fail to recover the knowledge. No chance-level reference is stated.
No recovery fine-tuning on unrelated, loosely related, or forgotten examples.
No activation-direction ablation or analysis establishing that unlearning blocks access rather than deleting knowledge.
No low-bit quantization of unlearned weights.
No prompt rephrasing, jailbreak, other-language, or in-context recovery test.
No evaluation of a counter-method's resistance to the recovery attacks in the claim.

relationships.reason: Surgical accuracy falls 89.2→17.3% (below 4-option chance) while L1–L3 and other-domain accuracy stay within ~1 point (T3-11, T3-12, T6-21–T6-24, T7-12).
relationships.display_finding: Surgical accuracy fell from 89.2% to 17.3%, below four-option chance, while other tested knowledge levels and domains stayed within about 1 point of baseline.

relation.reason: Its own results (target accuracy 89.2 to 17.3; retention within about 1 point; baselines lose 3.5-8.3 points) bear on whether A's first two parts hold. The 'attacks don't recover it' part is untested, but that leaves it untested and does not make it uses_without_test.

tranche.reason: A new medical setting (MedMCQA surgery, MHQA anxiety) with target and retained accuracy for its own method and for baselines. That bears on the first two parts of A. T3 is defensible, and T2 is also arguable.

source_check.notes: Values match Tables III, VI and VII (three seeds). No recovery attack is run, so B-F and A's robustness part are untested. Oddities: FR = 100 - L4 accuracy, yet the original model's FR is 0.0. Complete Retraining reaches L4 8.8%, far below 4-option chance. The paper states no chance level, and 17.3% below chance is not analysed.

statements.correction: This study: Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct (3B); target is MedMCQA surgical knowledge measured by MCQ accuracy. L4 surgical accuracy 89.2 to 17.3 (FR 82.7); KP 88.5 vs 89.2; L1-L3 within 1.3 points; MHQA other-MH KP 89.1 vs 87.6. Runs a membership-inference attack (AUC 0.555, MIA resistance 0.89) but no relearning, quantization, ablation or prompting recovery attack. Paper states no chance level. Belongs with the knowledge-accuracy studies.
statements.problem: Gives no numbers for this study, but cites it (T3-11) in a group of PII, task, code and behaviour targets. Its conditions say targets are not knowledge accuracy and models are 7-70B; neither is true here. 'REVS is the only study here that runs an attack' ignores this study's membership-inference evaluation (not a recovery attack). Citing it as support for A is right.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Reported unlearning and retention outcomes on MedMCQA and MHQA
reader_labels.reason: The methods reduce targeted-domain performance while reporting retained performance on non-target domains; see T3-03–T3-12, T6-05–T6-24, and T7-03–T7-12. These results do not test attack resistance.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Targeted-domain reduction in the reported evaluations
reader_labels.reason: The paper reports remaining target accuracy, including L4 accuracy of 17.3±2.1 and anxiety forgetting of 79.4±2.3, but states no chance-level reference; it also does not test whether attacks recover knowledge. See T3-11, T6-24, and T7-11.
